claim: Tonic pain after injury characterises a behavioural state that prioritises recovery.
source: Tonic pain after injury characterises a behavioural state that prioritises recovery.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Tonic pain generally suppresses cognition and attention.
source: Although generally suppressing cognition and attention, tonic pain needs to allow effective relief learning to reduce the cause of the pain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Active relief-seeking involves a reinforcement learning process manifest by error signals observed in the dorsal putamen.
source: In both studies, we show that active relief-seeking involves a reinforcement learning process manifest by error signals observed in the dorsal putamen.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both experiments showing dorsal putamen activation correlated with prediction errors.

claim: An uncertainty ('associability') signal is detected in pregenual anterior cingulate cortex that controls the relief learning rate.
source: Critically, this system uses an uncertainty ('associability') signal detected in pregenual anterior cingulate cortex that both controls the relief learning rate, and endogenously and parametrically modulates the level of tonic pain.
evidence: This is supported by neuroimaging data showing pgACC correlations with associability signals in both experiments.

claim: The associability signal endogenously and parametrically modulates the level of tonic pain.
source: Critically, this system uses an uncertainty ('associability') signal detected in pregenual anterior cingulate cortex that both controls the relief learning rate, and endogenously and parametrically modulates the level of tonic pain.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing negative correlation between associability and pain ratings.

claim: Decreased attention is seen in a range of cognitive tasks during tonic pain.
source: This effect extends to cognition, and decreased attention is seen in a range of cognitive tasks during tonic pain (Crombez et al., 1997; Lorenz and Bromm, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Perceived controllability has been found to reduce pain in some situations.
source: First, in some situations, perceived controllability has been found to reduce pain (Salomons et al., 2004; Salomons et al., 2007; Wiech et al., 2014; Becker et al., 2015), suggesting that the capacity to seek relief can engage endogenous modulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Instructed attention has commonly been observed to reduce pain.
source: Second, instructed attention has commonly been observed to reduce pain (Bantick et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Learning involves distinct processes of prediction ('state learning') and control ('action learning').
source: In general, learning involves distinct processes of prediction ('state learning') and control ('action learning') (Mackintosh, 1983), although relief learning during tonic pain has not been thoroughly investigated.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to classical learning theory.

claim: Relief learning during tonic pain has not been thoroughly investigated.
source: In general, learning involves distinct processes of prediction ('state learning') and control ('action learning') (Mackintosh, 1983), although relief learning during tonic pain has not been thoroughly investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: In the case of phasic pain, learning can be described by reinforcement learning (RL) models.
source: In the case of phasic pain, learning can be described by reinforcement learning (RL) models - a well-studied computational framework for learning from experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the text.

claim: RL models describe how to predict the occurrence of inherently salient events, and learn actions to exert control over them.
source: RL models describe how to predict the occurrence of inherently salient events, and learn actions to exert control over them (maximising rewards, minimising penalties) (Seymour et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a description of RL models supported by citation.

claim: High uncertainty corresponds to high attention and leads to more rapid learning.
source: Accordingly, high uncertainty corresponds to high attention and leads to more rapid learning (Dayan et al., 2000; Yu and Dayan, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational neuroscience literature.

claim: Associability calculates the running average of the magnitude of recent prediction errors.
source: One well-recognised way of formalising uncertainty in RL is by computing a quantity called the associability, which calculates the running average of the magnitude of recent prediction errors (i.e. frequent large prediction errors implies high uncertainty/associability).
evidence: This is a description of the computational implementation of associability.

claim: The concept of associability is grounded in classical theories of Pavlovian conditioning (the 'Pearce-Hall' learning rule).
source: The concept of associability is grounded in classical theories of Pavlovian conditioning (the 'Pearce-Hall' learning rule, Le Pelley, 2004; Pearce and Hall, 1980; Holland and Schiffino, 2016), and provides a good account of behaviour and neural responses during Pavlovian learning (Li et al., 2011; Boll et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to learning theory and empirical studies.

claim: Associability provides a good account of behaviour and neural responses during Pavlovian learning.
source: The concept of associability is grounded in classical theories of Pavlovian conditioning (the 'Pearce-Hall' learning rule, Le Pelley, 2004; Pearce and Hall, 1980; Holland and Schiffino, 2016), and provides a good account of behaviour and neural responses during Pavlovian learning (Li et al., 2011; Boll et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Experiment 1 was an escape learning task with fixed, probabilistic cue-relief contingencies.
source: Experiment 1 was an escape learning task (n = 19) with fixed, probabilistic cue-relief contingencies (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Each subject in Experiment 1 performed three instrumental sessions and three Pavlovian sessions.
source: Each subject performed three instrumental sessions and three Pavlovian sessions, to allow us to compare active and passive relief learning (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: During each session in Experiment 1, subjects were held in continuous pain by a thermal stimulator attached to their left arm.
source: During each session (lasting approximatey 5 min), subjects were held in continuous pain by a thermal stimulator attached to their left arm, and temporary relief (i.e. escape) was given by rapidly cooling the thermode for 4 s, after which it returned to the baseline tonic pain level (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Temporary relief in Experiment 1 was given by rapidly cooling the thermode for 4 s.
source: During each session (lasting approximatey 5 min), subjects were held in continuous pain by a thermal stimulator attached to their left arm, and temporary relief (i.e. escape) was given by rapidly cooling the thermode for 4 s, after which it returned to the baseline tonic pain level (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In instrumental sessions of Experiment 1, for one of the cues, the probability of relief was 80% for one action and 20% for the other action.
source: For one of the cues, the probability of relief was 80% for one action and 20% for the other action, and for the other cue, the action relief probabilities were 60% and 40%.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In instrumental sessions of Experiment 1, for the other cue, the action relief probabilities were 60% and 40%.
source: For one of the cues, the probability of relief was 80% for one action and 20% for the other action, and for the other cue, the action relief probabilities were 60% and 40%.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 1, choices were best fit by the basic TD model.
source: In a random-effects model comparison procedure (Daunizeau et al., 2014), we found that choices were best fit by the basic TD model (model frequency = 0.964, exceedance probability = 1, Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison statistics from behavioral data.

claim: There is no evidence that associability operates directly at the level of actions in Experiment 1.
source: Thus, there is no evidence that associability operates directly at the level of actions.
evidence: This is an inference from the model comparison results showing TD model fit better than hybrid action-learning model.

claim: In Experiment 1, SCRs obtained in instrumental sessions were higher compared to yoked Pavlovian sessions.
source: SCRs obtained in instrumental sessions were higher compared to yoked Pavlovian sessions (Figure 2b, n = 15, see Materials and methods for session exclusion criteria, paired t-test T(14)=2.55, p=0.023)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of SCR data between conditions.

claim: In Pavlovian aversive (fear) learning, SCRs have been shown to reflect the associability of Pavlovian predictions.
source: In Pavlovian aversive (fear) learning, SCRs have been shown to reflect the associability of Pavlovian predictions (Li et al., 2011; Boll et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In Experiment 1, a learning model with a state-based associability ('hybrid' model) best fit the SCR data in both Pavlovian and instrumental sessions.
source: Consistent with previous studies of phasic pain, model-fitting revealed that a learning model with a state-based associability ('hybrid' model) best fit the SCR data in both Pavlovian and instrumental sessions (Figure 2c and Figure 2d, instrumental sessions: model frequency = 0.436, exceedance probability = 0.648, Pavlovian sessions: model frequency = 0.545, exceedance probability = 0.676)
evidence: This is supported by model comparison statistics from SCR data.

claim: There is no support for a general effect of instrumental controllability on subjective pain and/or relief experience in Experiment 1.
source: Hence, there is no support for a general effect of instrumental controllability on subjective pain and/or relief experience.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of difference in ratings between instrumental and Pavlovian sessions.

claim: In Experiment 1, when relief was omitted, a larger frustrated (negative) relief prediction error was associated with an increase in pain.
source: That is, when relief was omitted (i.e. as was always the case on the pain rating trial), a larger frustrated (i.e. negative) relief prediction error was associated with an increase in pain - in contrast to the prediction of a placebo expectation hypothesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative correlation between prediction errors and pain ratings in Pavlovian sessions.

claim: In Experiment 1, the action prediction error from the TD model identified responses in bilateral putamen, bilateral amygdala, left DLPFC, and VMPFC.
source: This identified responses in bilateral putamen, bilateral amygdala, left DLPFC, and VMPFC (Figure 3a, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis showing brain regions correlated with the TD prediction error.

claim: In Experiment 1, Bayesian model selection showed that the action-learning TD model had higher posterior and exceedance probabilities in the dorsal putamen and VMPFC.
source: This showed that the action-learning TD model had higher posterior and exceedance probabilities in the dorsal putamen, and VMPFC (Figure 3b warm colour clusters).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian model selection analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Experiment 1, the state-learning (hybrid) model better explained activities in the amygdala, ventral striatum, and DLPFC.
source: The state-learning (hybrid) model better explained activities in the amygdala, ventral striatum, and DLPFC (Figure 3b cool colour clusters).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian model selection analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Experiment 1, BOLD responses correlated with trial-by-trial associability from the hybrid model were found only in pgACC in instrumental sessions.
source: We found correlated responses only in pgACC, in instrumental sessions (Figure 3d, Table 1, MNI coordinates of peak: [−2, 37, 5]).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis showing brain regions correlated with associability.

claim: In Experiment 1, no significant BOLD responses correlated with associability were observed in Pavlovian sessions.
source: No significant responses were observed in Pavlovian sessions.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of significant findings in the fMRI analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1, instrumental sessions had higher pgACC response magnitude compared to Pavlovian sessions across subjects.
source: Instrumental sessions had higher response magnitude in pgACC compared to Pavlovian sessions across subjects (Instrumental sessions: one-sample t-test against 0 T(18)=3.746, p=0.0015, Pavlovian sessions: one-sample t-test against 0 T(18)=-1.230, p=0.235, paired t-test for instrumental versus Pavlovian T(18)=3.317, p=0.0038).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of beta values extracted from pgACC ROI.

claim: In Experiment 2, 23 new subjects participated in a modified version of the instrumental escape learning task.
source: In Experiment 2, 23 new subjects participated in a modified version of the instrumental escape learning task in Experiment 1, with a number of important differences.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects performed only instrumental sessions.
source: First, subjects performed only instrumental sessions (8 sessions with 24 trials in each) given the absence of a global effect of instrumental versus Pavlovian pain in the first experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its rationale.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects were required to choose one out of three simultaneously presented visual cues to obtain relief.
source: Second, subjects were required to choose one out of three simultaneously presented visual cues to obtain relief, in which the position of each cue varied randomly from trial to trial.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, the action-outcome contingencies were non-stationary.
source: Third, the action-outcome contingencies were non-stationary, such that the relief probability from selecting each cue varied slowly throughout the experiment duration, controlled by a random walk algorithm which varied between 20 and 80% (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, the frequency of tonic pain ratings was increased to 10 per session.
source: Fourth, we increased the frequency of tonic pain ratings (10 per session, 80 per subject in total) to enhance power for identifying modulatory effects on pain.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its rationale.

claim: In Experiment 2, the rating was taken after the action but before outcome.
source: Fifth, the rating was taken after the action but before outcome, to provide an improved assessment of ongoing tonic pain modulation without interference by the outcome.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its rationale.

claim: In Experiment 2, SCRs were collected bilaterally.
source: Finally, we also collected SCRs bilaterally, to enhance the data quality given the importance of the SCR in inferences about associability.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its rationale.

claim: In Experiment 2, the basic TD action learning model best predicted choices following model comparison.
source: Despite the greater demands of the non-stationary task compared to Experiment 1, the basic TD action learning model still best predicted choices following model comparison (model frequency = 0.624, exceedance probability = 0.989)
evidence: This is supported by model comparison statistics from behavioral data.

claim: In Experiment 2, SCRs measured on the side with thermal stimulation (left hand) were lower than those on the side without stimulation (right hand).
source: The left side had lower mean SCRs (Figure 4b,L/R paired t-test T(19)=-2.67, p=0.015, n = 20, exclusion criteria followed from Experiment 1)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of SCR data between hands.

claim: In Experiment 2, the associability from the state-outcome hybrid model provided the best fit of trial-by-trial SCRs.
source: Using the same model-fitting procedure as in Experiment 1 (with the addition that the model now predicted SCR on both hands for each trial), we found that the associability from the state-outcome hybrid model again provided the best fit of trial-by-trial SCRs (Figure 4c, model frequency = 0.667, exceedance probability = 0.954).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison statistics from SCR data.

claim: In Experiment 2, the state-learning hybrid associability best fit the pain ratings.
source: In this analysis, the state-learning hybrid associability again best fit the pain ratings (model frequency = 0.698, exceedance probability = 0.980; n = 22, 1550 ratings, one participant was excluded for having >90% identical ratings).
evidence: This is supported by model comparison statistics from rating data.

claim: In Experiment 2, regression coefficients with hybrid model associability as uncertainty predictor were significant across subjects.
source: Regression coefficients with hybrid model associability as uncertainty predictor were significant across subjects (Figure 4e, one-sample t-test for three sets of coefficients: 'Relief' term: T(21)=-4.004, p<0.001 (i.e. habituation, reduced pain over time after relief), log(trial) term: T(21)=1.017, p=0.321, associability term: T(21)=-2.643, p=0.015).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of regression coefficients.

claim: In Experiment 2, the TD model action prediction errors were robustly correlated with BOLD responses in left dorsal putamen, bilateral amygdala, and left DLPFC.
source: We found that the TD model action prediction errors was robustly correlated with BOLD responses in similar regions identified in Experiment 1, including left dorsal putamen, bilateral amygdala, and left DLPFC (Figure 5a, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis showing brain regions correlated with the TD prediction error.

claim: In Experiment 2, Bayesian model selection showed the TD model had higher posterior and exceedance probabilities in the dorsal putamen, amygdala and DLPFC.
source: Of these, BMS showed the TD model had higher posterior and exceedance probabilities in the dorsal putamen, as well as amygdala and DLPFC (Figure 5b warm colour clusters).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian model selection analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Experiment 2, pgACC BOLD responses correlated with trial-by-trial associability from the state-learning hybrid model.
source: Following the same analysis as in Experiment 1, we found again that pgACC BOLD responses correlated with trial-by-trial associability from the state-learning hybrid model (Figure 5d–e, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis showing brain regions correlated with associability.

claim: In Experiment 2, the peak pgACC activation from associability analysis was almost identical to that in Experiment 1.
source: The peak from this analysis was almost identical to that in Experiment 1 (Overlayed clusters can be found in Figure supplements).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of peak coordinates between experiments.

claim: In Experiment 2, trial-by-trial pain ratings as a parametric modulator did not reveal significant pgACC responses.
source: In addition, we used trial-by-trial pain ratings as a parametric modulator, but did not find significant pgACC responses, which suggested that it was unlikely to be solely driven by pain perception itself.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of significant findings in the fMRI analysis and its interpretation.

claim: Relief seeking from the state of tonic pain is supported by a reinforcement learning process, in which optimal escape actions are acquired using prediction error signals observed in the dorsal putamen.
source: First, we show that relief seeking from the state of tonic pain is supported by a reinforcement learning process, in which optimal escape actions are acquired using prediction error signals, which are observed as BOLD signals in the dorsal putamen.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined results from both experiments.

claim: During learning, the level of ongoing pain is reduced by the learned associability associated with state-based relief predictions.
source: Second, we show that during learning, the level of ongoing pain is reduced by the learned associability associated with state-based relief predictions.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined results from both experiments.

claim: The associability signal that reduces pain is associated with BOLD responses in the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex.
source: This signal thus reduces pain when there is a greater capacity to learn new information and is associated with BOLD responses in the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined results from both experiments.

claim: The results identify a learning circuit that governs tonic pain escape learning whilst also suppressing pain according to the precise information available during learning.
source: Together, these results identify a learning circuit that governs tonic pain escape learning whilst also suppressing pain according to the precise information available during learning.
evidence: This is a summary claim integrating the findings from both experiments.

claim: The findings highlight the dual function of a state-based relief associability signal during tonic pain escape.
source: The findings highlight the dual function of a state-based relief associability signal during tonic pain escape.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the main findings.

claim: Associability has its theoretical underpinnings in classical theories of associative learning and attention (i.e. the Pearce-Hall theory).
source: Associability has its theoretical underpinnings in classical theories of associative learning and attention (i.e. the Pearce-Hall theory, Pearce and Hall, 1980), and its mathematical implementation here is as an approximate uncertainty quantity derived from computing the running average of the magnitude of the prediction error (Sutton, 1992; Le Pelley, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to learning theory literature.

claim: When uncertainty is high (because of lots of recent large prediction errors), associability increases the speed of acquisition through increasing the learning rate.
source: This uncertainty signal effectively captures how predictable the environment is: when uncertainty is high (because of lots of recent large prediction errors), it increases the speed of acquisition through increasing the learning rate, and so accelerates convergence to stable predicted values.
evidence: This is an explanation of how associability functions in learning.

claim: Associability is an effective attention-like signal for mediating endogenous analgesia because it selectively facilitates active relief seeking by suppressing pain only when it is necessary.
source: It is therefore an effective attention-like signal for mediating endogenous analgesia, because it selectively facilitates active relief seeking by suppressing pain only when it is necessary.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Uncertainty enhances phasic pain where pain acts as the signal to drive learning.
source: This conception of the role of uncertainty in pain may explain why uncertainty has been shown to enhance phasic pain (Yoshida et al., 2013) - where pain acts as the signal to drive learning, and suppresses tonic pain, where pain acts to reduce general cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and provides an interpretation of how uncertainty affects different types of pain.

claim: Uncertainty suppresses tonic pain, where pain acts to reduce general cognition.
source: This conception of the role of uncertainty in pain may explain why uncertainty has been shown to enhance phasic pain (Yoshida et al., 2013) - where pain acts as the signal to drive learning, and suppresses tonic pain, where pain acts to reduce general cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the current findings.

claim: In both instances (phasic and tonic pain), the role of uncertainty and attention is to facilitate learning.
source: In both instances, the role of uncertainty and attention is to facilitate learning.
evidence: This is a general interpretive statement about the function of uncertainty.

claim: Associability cannot distinguish unreliable cues - inherently poor predictors of outcomes.
source: A caveat to this is that associability cannot distinguish unreliable cues - inherently poor predictors of outcomes, and so does not discriminate between reducible and irreducible uncertainty
evidence: This is a theoretical limitation of the associability mechanism.

claim: Associability does not discriminate between reducible and irreducible uncertainty.
source: A caveat to this is that associability cannot distinguish unreliable cues - inherently poor predictors of outcomes, and so does not discriminate between reducible and irreducible uncertainty
evidence: This is a theoretical limitation of the associability mechanism.

claim: In rodent studies of associative learning, associability is maintained even after several days of training.
source: However, in rodent studies of associative learning, associability is maintained even after several days of training (Holland et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to animal learning research.

claim: The localisation of the associability signal to the pgACC is consistent with a priori predictions.
source: The localisation of the associability signal to the pgACC is consistent with a priori predictions.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of findings with prior hypotheses.

claim: The pgACC region is known to be involved in threat unpredictability.
source: The region is known to be involved in threat unpredictability (Rubio et al., 2015; Nitschke et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The pgACC is involved in computations of uncertainty during difficult approach-avoidance decision-making.
source: computations of uncertainty during difficult approach-avoidance decision-making (Amemori and Graybiel, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The pgACC is involved in the perseverance of behaviour during foraging.
source: and in the perseverance of behaviour during foraging (McGuire and Kable, 2015; Kolling et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The pgACC has been specifically implicated in various forms of endogenous analgesia, including coping with uncontrollable pain.
source: More importantly, it has been specifically implicated in various forms of endogenous analgesia, including coping with uncontrollable pain (Salomons et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The pgACC has been implicated in distraction-related analgesia.
source: distraction (Valet et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The pgACC has been implicated in placebo analgesia.
source: and placebo analgesia (Bingel et al., 2006; Eippert et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The pgACC has been suggested to be central to a 'medial pain system' and the descending control of pain.
source: The pgACC has been suggested to be central to a 'medial pain system' and the descending control of pain, with its known anatomical and functional connectivity to key regions including the amygdala (Derbyshire et al., 1997; Vogt et al., 2005; Salomons et al., 2015) and PAG (Stein et al., 2012; Buchanan et al., 1994; Vogt, 2005; Domesick, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroanatomical and functional connectivity studies.

claim: The results provide a formal computational framework that brings together theories of pain attention, controllability and endogenous analgesia.
source: The results provide a formal computational framework that brings together theories of pain attention, controllability and endogenous analgesia.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the theoretical contribution of the work.

claim: Previous demonstrations of reduced pain have been inconsistent.
source: Previous demonstrations of reduced pain (albeit typically for phasic, not tonic pain) have been inconsistent (Becker et al., 2015; Salomons et al., 2004; Salomons et al., 2007; Wiech et al., 2014; Wiech et al., 2006; Mohr et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research showing mixed results.

claim: Endogenous analgesia is not a non-specific manifestation of control, but rather a specific process linked to the learnable information.
source: Our results offer insight into why - by suggesting that endogenous analgesia is not a non-specific manifestation of control, but rather a specific process linked to the learnable information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of previous literature.

claim: Motivation during the persistent pain state can be understood as an escape learning problem.
source: From the perspective of animal learning theory, the experiments here show how motivation during the persistent pain state can be understood as an escape learning problem, in which the state of relief is determined by the offset of a tonic aversive state (Mackintosh, 1983; Solomon and Corbit, 1974).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of learning theory, supported by citations.

claim: Escape learning is theoretically distinct from relief that results from omission of otherwise expected pain or punishment.
source: This is theoretically distinct from the better-studied form of relief that results from omission of otherwise expected pain or punishment (Konorski, 1967), and which motivates avoidance behaviour (Mowrer, 1960).
evidence: This is a theoretical distinction supported by citations to learning theory.

claim: Acquisition of dissociable behavioural responses (SCRs and choices) reveals the underlying theoretical architecture of the escape learning process, which involves both parallel state-outcome and action-outcome learning components.
source: In our task, acquisition of dissociable behavioural responses (SCRs and choices) reveals the underlying theoretical architecture of the escape learning process, which involves both parallel state-outcome and action-outcome learning components.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings showing different learning mechanisms for different behavioral measures.

claim: The action-outcome learning error signal localises to a region of the dorsolateral striatum (dorsal putamen).
source: The action-outcome learning error signal localises to a region of the dorsolateral striatum (dorsal putamen).
evidence: This is a summary of the neuroimaging findings.

claim: Striatal error signals are seen across a broad range of action learning tasks.
source: Striatal error signals are seen across a broad range of action learning tasks, although the region here appears more dorsolateral than previously noted in avoidance learning (Kim et al., 2006; Seymour et al., 2012; Delgado et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and comparison with current findings.

claim: There are multiple error signals in dorsal and ventral striatum, reflecting 'model-based' (cognitive), 'model-free' (including stimulus-response habits) and Pavlovian control.
source: But it is well recognised that there are multiple error signals in dorsal and ventral striatum, for instance reflecting 'model-based' (cognitive), 'model-free' (including stimulus-response habits) and Pavlovian control (Tricomi et al., 2009; Schonberg et al., 2010; Yin et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on striatal function.

claim: The reinforcement learning model described is a 'model-free' mechanism, since it learns action values but does not build an internal model of state-outcome identities and transition probabilities.
source: The reinforcement learning model we describe is a 'model-free' mechanism, since it learns action values but does not build an internal model of state-outcome identities and transition probabilities (Daw et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a characterization of the computational model used, supported by citation.

claim: A model-based system likely co-exists with the model-free system and might be identifiable with appropriate task designs.
source: However, it is likely that a model-based system co-exists and might be identifiable with appropriate task designs (Daw et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation about additional learning systems, supported by citation.

claim: Adaptive learning processes are thought to be important in chronic pain.
source: Adaptive learning processes are thought to be important in chronic pain: learning and controllability have been proposed to play a role in the pathogenesis and maintenance of chronic pain (Vlaeyen, 2015; Flor et al., 2002; Apkarian et al., 2004; Salomons et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to chronic pain literature.

claim: Brain regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex and striatum have been consistently implicated in clinical studies of chronic pain.
source: and brain regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex and striatum have been consistently implicated in clinical studies, for example in pain offset responses (Baliki et al., 2010) and resting functional connectivity in chronic back pain (Baliki et al., 2008; Baliki et al., 2012; Fritz et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical neuroimaging studies.

claim: The results highlight the pgACC as a potential target for therapeutic intervention in chronic pain.
source: In addition to suggesting a possible computational mechanism that might underlie pain susceptibility in these patients, the results highlight the pgACC as a potential target for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a speculation about clinical implications of the findings.

claim: In Experiment 1, the temperature of painful tonic stimuli was set according to the subject's own pain threshold calibrated beforehand.
source: The temperature of painful tonic stimuli was set according to the subject's own pain threshold calibrated beforehand.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In Experiment 1, the relief temperature was set constant at 13°C below threshold temperature for all subjects.
source: The relief temperature was set constant at 13°C below threshold temperature for all subjects.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In Experiment 1, functional images were collected with a single echo EPI sequence with TR = 2500 ms, TE = 30 ms, flip angle = 80, field of view = 240 mm.
source: functional images were collected with a single echo EPI sequence (repetition time TR = 2500 ms, echo time TE = 30 ms, flip angle = 80, field of view = 240 mm)
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: In both experiments, 37 contiguous oblique-axial slices (voxel size 3.75 × 3.75×3.75 mm) parallel to the AC-PC line were acquired.
source: 37 contiguous oblique-axial slices (voxel size 3.75 × 3.75×3.75 mm) parallel to the AC-PC line were acquired.
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition parameters.
